content: Several studies were conducted to evaluate the use of mobile stock notification systems in healthcare settings. Most of these studies were carried out in countries such as Liberia, Uganda, South Africa, and India. The primary goal of these interventions was to make stock-level data and potential stock-out risks visible to healthcare managers, enabling them to take corrective actions to address shortages. Key factors influencing the implementation of mobile stock notification systems were identified. These included infrastructural challenges, such as limited access to electricity and poor internet connectivity (moderate confidence), and broader health system issues, such as national-level drug shortages that could not be resolved at the primary healthcare level (low confidence). Other important factors included the availability of stock-level data across all levels of the health system (low confidence), the training and familiarity of healthcare providers with digital devices (moderate confidence), the availability of technical expertise for system development and maintenance (low confidence), user-friendly system design with input from end-users (moderate confidence), and the presentation of data in accessible formats, such as interactive dashboards (moderate confidence). Supportive supervision was also emphasized as critical for the effective adoption of digital systems (moderate confidence). In Malawi, a study compared mobile stock notification systems with enhanced management to standard care in primary healthcare settings. The intervention involved quality improvement teams using data from the notification system to manage stock. However, the evidence regarding the impact of this approach on stock-outs of essential medicines, such as Cotrimoxazole, was assessed as very low certainty. Similarly, the quality and timeliness of stock management data, as well as provider satisfaction with the system, were also evaluated with very low certainty due to methodological limitations and small sample sizes. The use of mobile stock notification systems with effective product transport was also studied in Malawi. This intervention included training health surveillance assistants and providing tools for bicycle maintenance to improve product delivery. However, the evidence on the impact of this approach on stock-outs, data quality, and lead times for fulfilling orders was also of very low certainty. Overall, the studies highlighted the need for more robust research to assess the effectiveness of mobile stock notification systems and the factors influencing their implementation. Challenges such as infrastructural limitations, lack of national-level stock availability, and the need for user-friendly systems and adequate training were consistently identified as barriers to successful implementation.
